title: Cap. XI: Mediate imputation owned; Origen witnesses used against Garissoles
pass_a_gloss: Do we hold the same as those heretics? On the contrary, we contradict them. For we believe and teach that there can be some just imputation of another's sin; and we admit the imputation of the first Adam's own sin as consequent or mediate. Add that their heresy was situated not in that opinion, but in the most absurd dogma they were busy proving from it. Therefore the two witnesses Lord Garissoles praises — Origen, Homily 8 on Exodus, and Jerome's Commentary on Ezekiel 18:1–2 — he praises both against himself. For when Origen had brought forward those words which Garissoles quotes — Let us see how the sins of the fathers are said to be visited on the sons into the third and fourth generation. For in this saying heretics are accustomed to taunt us, that it is not the speech of a good God who says another is punished for another's sins — Does Origen answer what Garissoles would have answered, that this is by no means unjust? No: since he thought it unjust and wholly unbecoming to God, he fled to a metaphorical sense, and wanted the parents to be understood as the Devil and his angels, the sons and first generation as those the Devil immediately seduces, the second as those next seduced by these, the third and fourth as those whom these join to themselves as partners or servants of sin. But these men, sons of the devil, are seized and punished in this age that they may be saved; yet the punishment of the demons who are their parents is deferred to the age to come.
pass_b_english: Do we agree with those heretics? On the contrary, we contradict them. We believe and teach that some just imputation of another's sin is possible, and we admit the imputation of Adam's first sin as consequent or mediate. Their heresy did not sit in that opinion, but in the absurd dogma they tried to prove from it. So the two witnesses Garissoles cites — Origen's eighth homily on Exodus, and Jerome on Ezekiel 18:1–2 — he cites against himself. When Origen had offered the words Garissoles quotes — how the fathers' sins are said to be visited on the children to the third and fourth generation, a saying heretics use to taunt us as unworthy of a good God who punishes one for another's sins — does Origen answer as Garissoles would, that this is not unjust at all? No. Thinking it unjust and unfit for God, he fled to metaphor: the 'parents' are the Devil and his angels; the first generation, those the Devil seduces directly; the second, those next seduced by them; the third and fourth, those they recruit as partners or servants of sin. Those human sons of the devil are seized and punished in this age so they may be saved; the demons who are their parents have their punishment deferred to the age to come.
source_text: Nos-ne idem cum illis haereticis sentimus? Imo eis contradicimus. Aliquam enim esse posse justam alieni peccati imputationem credimus, & docemus; ipsiusque primi Adae peccati imputationem admittimus consequentem seu mediatam. Adde quod non in ea sententia, sed in dogmate, quod inde probare satagebant, absurdissimo eorum sita erat haeresis. Itaque quos duos testes laudat D. G. Origenem hom. 8. in Exod. & Hieronymum Comm. in Ezech. xviii. 1. 2. eos ambos laudat contra se. Cum enim Origenes protulisset illa verba, quae D. G. recitat — Videamus quomodo reddi dicantur peccata patrum in filios in tertiam & quartam generationem. In hoc enim sermone solent nos haeretici suggillare, quod non sit boni Dei sermo, qui pro peccatis alterius alterum plecti dicat — Respondet-ne, id quod D. G. respondisset, hoc minime esse injustum? Imo cum injustum id putaret, minimeque Deum decere, confugit ad sensum metaphoricum, & per parentes intelligi voluit Diabolum & angelos eius, per filios ac primam generationem eos quos Diabolus immediate seducit, per secundam eos qui ab his proxime seducuntur, per tertiam & quartam eos quos hi vel socios, vel administros peccati sibi adjungunt. Hos autem homines filios diaboli corripi & puniri in hoc saeculo, ut serventur: diabolorum vero, qui sunt eorum parentes, supplicium differri in futurum saeculum.

choices.why: Origen/Jerome do not support Garissoles's immediate-imputation reading
